pseudoStyles.ariaLabel: Three ways to write the same thing

notes.platform: Procedure, For each and End If spell the structure out in full, which suits readers who do not know a particular language.

what-is-dsa.title: What Are Algorithms and Data Structures
what-is-dsa.subtitle: Understand what this platform teaches

comparisons.label: Algorithm
comparisons.description: "How to do it": a set of clear steps that solves a problem, such as searching, sorting and traversing (looking at every item once). To guess a number from 1 to 100, guessing 1, 2, 3, … takes up to 100 tries in the worst case, while always guessing the middle takes at most 7. Learning algorithms means learning to pick the fast and cheap one.

comparisons.label: Data structure
comparisons.description: "Where it lives": a way of organizing and storing data, which decides how data is placed, found and changed. A stack only gives you the top book, a queue is first in first out, and a tree is followed down by category. No arrangement is always best; it depends on what you do most often.

comparisons.label: Together they set the speed
comparisons.description: A good method paired with a suitable arrangement is fast and cheap. With the wrong arrangement, even clever steps are slow.

slides.title: Data structures you will learn here
How to learn on this platform
items: Watch the animation — see step by step how the data changes. This is the "how"
Read the code — pseudo code and Python side by side, so you know what each line does
Do the practice — questions check that you really understood, not just watched
Learn complexity — animations show the steps but not "what it costs". That is what the next lessons are about

slides.title: Key takeaways
items: An algorithm is a set of clear steps that solves a problem
A data structure is a way of organizing and storing data
Together they decide how efficient a program is
Animations show you how. Complexity tells you whether it is worth it

read-code.title: Reading Example Code
read-code.subtitle: Understanding the Python used on this platform is enough

slides.title: You do not need to write it, just read it
slides.body:
Every example on this platform is written in Python. You do not need to be able to write programs. If you can read what each line does, you can follow the animations and the complexity that come later.

This lesson covers only five things:
• Variables: names for data
• Lists: a row of data you pick from by number
• Loops: do a piece of code again and again
• Conditions: do something only if it holds
• Functions: wrap code up and give it a name

Look up any other syntax when you meet it; there is no need to memorize it all at once.

slides.title: Variables: names for data
slides.code:
count = 3                 # a number
name = "CodePulse"        # text
nums = [4, 8, 15]         # a list: a row of data
count = count + 1         # a variable can change: count is now 4
slides.body:
"=" is not the "equals" of maths. It means "put the value on the right into the name on the left".
So count = count + 1 means: work out the right side (3 + 1) first, then put the result back into count.

slides.title: Lists and indexes: pick by number
slides.code:
nums = [4, 8, 15, 16]
nums[0]       # 4: the index starts at 0, so nums[0] is the first
nums[2]       # 15
nums[-1]      # 16: -1 means the last one
len(nums)     # 4: how many items
slides.body:
An index is the number of the position, counted from 0.
With a number you can take the item at any position directly, without searching from the start.

slides.title: Loops: repeat a piece of code
slides.code:
total = 0
for x in nums:        # take one item from nums into x each time
    total += x        # total += x means total = total + x

for i in range(3):    # i is 0, 1, 2: it runs 3 times
    print(i)

n = 8
while n > 1:          # repeat as long as the condition holds
    n = n // 2        # // is whole-number division: 8 → 4 → 2 → 1
slides.body:
When you see for, ask first: "how many times will it run?" for means "do it once for each item", while means "keep doing it as long as the condition holds".
Indentation (the spaces at the start of a line) shows that the line is inside the loop.

slides.title: Conditions: do it only if it holds
slides.body:
if, elif and else are checked in order. The first one that holds runs and the rest are skipped.
"=" puts a value in, while "==" compares two sides. Do not mix them up.

slides.title: Functions: wrap it up and name it
slides.code:
def total(nums):            # define a function called total that takes nums
    result = 0
    for x in nums:
        result += x
    return result           # hand the result back

print(total([4, 8, 15]))    # call it: prints 27
slides.body:
def defines a function and return hands the result back to where it was called. A function only runs when it is called.
Names you will see later, such as total and find_max, are all functions.

slides.title: Four habits for reading code
items: Read the function name and its parameters first — know what data it takes and what it returns
Find the loops — how many times a loop runs is the number of steps you will count in the next lesson
Track the variables — run it one line at a time and note how each variable changes
Watch the indentation — lines with the same indentation belong together, and a line pushed to the right is inside

slides.title: Run it one line at a time
Key takeaways
items: A variable is a name, and "=" puts the right-hand value into it
A list is picked by number, and numbering starts at 0
for does something once per item, while repeats as long as the condition holds
if checks a condition and == is the comparison; def defines a function and return hands back the result

pseudocode.title: Pseudocode
pseudocode.subtitle: Write down the steps of an algorithm in near-everyday language

slides.title: What is pseudocode
slides.body:
Pseudocode is a set of steps written for people. It looks like a program, but it belongs to no programming language and a computer will not run it.

It helps because:
• You can work out "how to do it" first and worry about syntax later
• The same pseudocode can be written in Python, Java or any other language
• Every algorithm animation on this platform shows pseudocode next to Python

There is no single standard way to write it: this platform uses Procedure, If … Then, For each … Do and While … Do, and writes ← for "put into".
When you write your own, any style will do as long as a reader can follow it.

rows: For each x in nums Do
Do it once for each item
Keep repeating while the condition holds
table.note:
In pseudocode, If, For and While each have an End If, End For and End While that mark where the block ends; Python shows it with indentation instead.
This is only the platform's habit. You do not have to copy it when you write your own, and the next slides show other ways.

slides.title: Example: find the maximum
slides.code:
Procedure FindMax(nums):
  biggest ← nums[0]
  For each x in nums Do
    If x > biggest Then
      biggest ← x
    End If
  End For
  Return biggest
End Procedure
slides.body:
Indentation shows "which level it belongs to", and End If and End For mark where a block ends.
"←" reads "put into": biggest ← x puts x into biggest.
This is the same thing as finding the maximum in "Run it one line at a time" in the previous lesson.

slides.title: You do not have to copy the platform style
Turning pseudocode into Python
slides.body:
Turning pseudocode into Python is mostly a change of spelling:
• ← becomes =
• If … Then becomes if …:, and the closing End If is dropped in favor of indentation
• For each x in nums Do becomes for x in nums:
• While … Do becomes while …:
• Procedure name(parameters) becomes def name(parameters):
• To compare two things, pseudocode writes = and Python writes ==

Every End … (End If, End For, End While, End Procedure) has no line of its own in Python; the block ends when the indentation goes back to the left.

slides.title: How to write pseudocode yourself
items: Say the goal in one sentence — what comes in and what you want out
Write every step down and ignore syntax — it only has to be clear to a reader, so focus on order and conditions
Use indentation for levels — steps inside a loop or condition move to the right
Run it by hand on a small example — check the result step by step and find the cases you missed

slides.title: Key takeaways
items: Pseudocode is steps written for people and belongs to no programming language
You can choose your own style, as long as a reader can follow it and no step is missing
The platform writes it with Procedure, If, For each, While and ←
To turn it into Python, ← becomes = and End … becomes indentation
Work out the steps first and worry about syntax later

big-o-basics.title: What Is Big-O
big-o-basics.subtitle: Describe the cost of a program with O()

slides.title: Why not just measure seconds?
slides.body:
The most natural way to compare two algorithms is to measure how long they run.

But seconds depend on many things:
• How fast the computer is
• Which programming language is used
• How many other programs are running

The same code can take very different time on someone else's machine. So we ask a different question:
When the amount of data grows, how many more steps does the program take?

slides.title: Count the steps
slides.code:
def total(nums):
    result = 0          # runs once
    for x in nums:      # the loop runs n times
        result += x     # a fixed few steps each time, n times in all
    return result       # runs once
slides.body:
With n items the loop runs n times, so the total is a few times n plus a little extra.
When the data becomes 10 times larger, the steps become about 10 times larger. That is "proportional to n", written O(n).

slides.title: Two simplification rules
items: Ignore constant factors — 2n, 100n and n/2 all simplify to O(n). When data grows, the trend is what matters
Keep only the fastest-growing term — n² + n + 1 simplifies to O(n²). For large n the other terms are too small to matter
Examples — 3n + 5 is O(n); n² + 100n is O(n²); a fixed 7 steps is O(1)

rows: Reading by index, arr[3]: no matter how long the array is, the position is computed directly
Finding the maximum: every element must be checked once to be sure
Two nested loops: every element is paired with every element
table.note: O(n) is read "Big-O of n". It means the number of steps grows at most roughly in proportion to n. Big-O describes the trend of growth, not an exact number of seconds.

slides.title: Key takeaways
items: Instead of seconds, look at how steps grow as the data grows
Big-O ignores constant factors and keeps the fastest-growing term
O(1) is a fixed number of steps, O(n) grows with the data, O(n²) grows with its square
Big-O describes a trend, not an exact number of seconds

growth-rates.title: Common Growth Rates
growth-rates.subtitle: See how far apart O(1) and O(2ⁿ) really are

slides.title: How big is the gap as n grows

rows: longer than the age of the universe
table.note: Numbers are approximate step counts; log is base 2. Time assumes a computer doing one billion steps per second. With little data you cannot tell the difference; with a lot of data the gap goes from "a bit slower" to "impossible".

slides.title: Drag n and see the gap
What each growth rate looks like ①
slides.code:
def first(arr):             # O(1): one step no matter the length
    return arr[0]

def total(arr):             # O(n): touch every element once
    s = 0
    for x in arr:
        s += x
    return s
slides.body: Reading one value is O(1). Walking from start to end is O(n).

slides.title: What each growth rate looks like ②
slides.body:
O(n log n) is common for "split in half, process, then merge", such as merge sort.
O(2ⁿ) becomes unusably slow with even a modest n.

rows: No loop, just reading a value
The range is halved each time
Binary search: one million items take only about 20 steps
One loop over all the data
Split in half, process, then merge
Two loops that each run n times
Bubble, selection and insertion sort: ten times the data, a hundred times the time
One call splits into two calls and nothing is reused
table.note: This is only a first guess. Real questions still need the details.

slides.title: Key takeaways
items: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2ⁿ)
With little data the gap is small. With a lot of data it decides whether the program is usable
Counting loop levels and how the range shrinks gives a quick guess of the growth rate
Binary search is O(log n), advanced sorts are O(n log n), basic sorts are O(n²)

case-analysis.title: Best, Worst and Average Case
case-analysis.subtitle: Why one algorithm can have different answers

slides.title: One algorithm, different inputs
items: Best case — the input that favors the algorithm most. Linear search: the target is first, O(1)
Worst case — the input that hurts the algorithm most. Linear search: the target is last or missing, O(n)
Average case — the typical performance over all possible inputs. Linear search: about half the array, roughly n/2 steps, still O(n)
slides.body: The same algorithm can be much faster on some inputs than on others. Take "looking for a number in an array from the start" (called linear search): if you are lucky it is the first one; if not, it is the last, or not in the array at all, and you still look at everything. So "how long does searching take" is not enough. You also need to say which case you mean:

slides.title: Why the worst case is used so often
slides.body:
The worst case is a guarantee: however bad the input, the time will not exceed it.

That is why it is the case you will look at most when learning and comparing algorithms.
A question usually says which case it means. When it does not, think of the worst case first.

The best case is too optimistic, and the average case needs to know how the inputs are distributed, which is not always easy.

slides.title: Example: bubble sort with early exit
slides.body:
Bubble sort keeps comparing two neighbors and swaps them when they are in the wrong order.
Already sorted data stops after one pass with no swaps: best case O(n).
Completely reversed data swaps in every pass: worst case O(n²).
Same code, and the two cases differ by a factor of n.

slides.title: Example: the shape of a BST

comparisons.label: A balanced BST
comparisons.description: In a BST (binary search tree), every node has smaller values on its left and larger values on its right, so each step down discards one side. When the tree is balanced, each step discards half of the nodes, the height (how many levels deep it goes) is about log n, and search is O(log n).

comparisons.label: A degenerate BST
comparisons.description: Insert 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 in order and the tree becomes a line. The height is n, so search degrades to O(n).

comparisons.label: How to avoid it
comparisons.description: Self-balancing trees such as AVL and red-black trees adjust their shape automatically, keeping even the worst case at O(log n).

slides.title: Key takeaways
items: One algorithm can have different complexity on different inputs
Best, worst and average case are stated separately
When nothing is said, think of the worst case first
Sorted input and a degenerate BST are common sources of the gap between best and worst case

space-complexity.title: Space Complexity and the Call Stack
space-complexity.subtitle: Count the extra memory

slides.title: What is space complexity
slides.body:
Time complexity asks "how many steps". Space complexity asks "how much more memory".

Most textbooks and questions count only the extra space: what the algorithm allocates on its own, such as new arrays and dictionaries, plus the data kept on the stack during recursion (a function calling itself), which you will see below.

The input itself is usually not counted.

slides.title: The difference between O(1) and O(n)
slides.body:
total uses one extra variable no matter how long nums is.
doubled builds a new list as long as the input, so its extra space grows with n.

slides.title: Recursion uses space too
slides.body:
Every time a function calls itself, the computer puts one more layer on the call stack to remember what to do when it returns.
factorial(5) calls all the way down to factorial(1), so the stack is 5 layers deep.
So the recursive factorial uses O(n) extra space even though the code declares no array.

comparisons.label: Iterative binary search
comparisons.description: It only keeps left, right and mid, so the extra space is O(1).

comparisons.label: Recursive binary search
comparisons.description: Each call handles half of the range and the stack gets at most log n layers deep, so the extra space is O(log n).

comparisons.label: Recursive DFS (go as deep as possible, then back up) on a degenerate tree
comparisons.description: When the tree is a line, the recursion depth equals the number of nodes, so the extra space is O(n).

slides.title: Common misunderstandings
slides.body:
• "No array declared" does not mean O(1): the recursion call stack counts too
• "Fast in time" does not mean "small in space": merge sort is O(n log n) in time but needs O(n) extra space
• In-place algorithms change the input directly and use O(1) extra space: bubble, selection and insertion sort all do

Time and space are often a trade-off: a little more memory can buy more speed.

slides.title: Key takeaways
items: Space complexity counts the extra memory, not the input itself
The depth of the recursion call stack counts too
Iterative versions usually use less space than recursive ones
Time and space are often a trade-off

multi-variable-complexity.title: Describing Complexity with Several Variables
multi-variable-complexity.subtitle: V, E, tree height h, and a cheat sheet

slides.title: Why n is not always enough
slides.body:
Some problems have more than one "size".
• A graph has vertices and edges
• A two-dimensional map has rows and columns
• How fast a tree is depends on its height, not on the number of nodes

In these cases complexity needs several variables, otherwise it is misleading.

slides.title: Common variables
items: V — the number of vertices in a graph
E — the number of edges in a graph. BFS and DFS (two ways to walk through a graph) look at each vertex and each edge once, so the time is O(V + E)
h — the height of a tree. About log n when balanced and n when degenerate, so BST operations are O(h)
R × C — rows and columns of a grid. Visiting the whole map is O(R × C)

comparisons.label: BFS / DFS
comparisons.description: Each vertex is visited once and each edge is checked once, so time is O(V + E). The queue or stack holds at most all the vertices, so space is O(V).

comparisons.label: BST search
comparisons.description: Each step down drops part of the nodes, so the steps are proportional to the height h and the time is O(h): O(log n) on average, O(n) in the worst case.

comparisons.label: Dijkstra
comparisons.description: Dijkstra finds shortest paths. It is O((V + E) log V) with a min-heap (a structure that gives the minimum quickly), and O(V²) when the minimum is found by scanning an array.

slides.title: How to store vertices and edges

rows: Search O(n); read by index O(1)
table.note: The BST worst case happens when the tree degenerates into a line.

rows: Average O(n log n) / worst O(n²)
table.note: These agree with each level's tutorial. See the matching level for details.

slides.title: Key takeaways
items: When a problem has several sizes, describe complexity with several variables
Graphs use V and E, trees use height h, grids use R × C
The cheat sheet quickly compares common structures and algorithms
When unsure, go back to the basics: count the steps and read the loops
